Theme

School & learning

education noun

also schooling, upbringing, educate, educated, uneducated, scholarly, learned, accomplished

classical

Cic. de Or. 2.1: prīma illa puerīlī īnstitūtiōne
Traupman 29, 308
Traupman 30: instruction
Traupman 333

īnstitūtiō, īnstitūtiōnis f.

noun, third declension

education, teaching, training

Teaching and training at any age: Quintilian’s Īnstitūtiō ōrātōria is the orator’s education. To educate is īnstituere or ērudīre; educated, ērudītus; uneducated, inērudītus or indoctus (Traupman 29, 152, 158, 308, 400).

Other words

  • ēducātiō, ēducātiōnis f. — upbringing; the education of a child

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Quint. 1.10.18: quae in ēducātiōnem contulerit; Cic. de Or. 3.125: īnstitūtus līberāliter ēducātiōne doctrīnāque puerīlī

    The bringing-up of a child, at home and at school: Quintilian’s old man counts what he paid the music and geometry teachers among the costs of the boy’s ēducātiō (1.10.18). Strictly it is rearing, of children and of animals (Traupman 29): ēdūcit obstetrīx, ēducat nūtrīx, īnstituit paedagōgus, docet magister (Varro ap. Non. 447, Lewis & Short s.v. ēducō).

  • disciplīna, disciplīnae f. — teaching, training; a system of education

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 4.3: disciplīnam puerīlem ingenuīs

    Disciplīna puerīlis is Cicero’s phrase for the schooling of freeborn children, which the Romans, unlike the Greeks, never fixed by law (Rep. 4.3).

  • doctrīna, doctrīnae f. — teaching; the learning it gives

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 2.13; Cic. de Or. 3.125: doctrīnāque puerīlī

  • ērudītiō, ērudītiōnis f. — instruction; learning, the education a person has

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14; Cic. de Or. 2.1: omnis ērudītiōnis expertem; Traupman 308, 152

    Far more often the learning that instruction leaves than the instruction itself (Lewis & Short).

  • ērudiō, ērudīre, ērudīvī, ērudītum — educate, instruct

    verb, fourth conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.4: studiōsōs discendī ērudiunt atque docent (Lewis & Short); Traupman 308

  • ērudītus, ērudīta, ērudītum — educated, learned

    also used · classical · Traupman 308

  • īnstituō, īnstituere, īnstituī, īnstitūtum — educate, train, bring up

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Traupman 308

Examples

  • Cicerō noster dum ego absum nōn cessāvit apud rhētorem. dē ejus ērudītiōne quod labōrēs nihil est, quoniam ingenium ejus nōstī, studium ego videō.

    Our Cicero has not been idle at his rhetoric teacher’s while I’ve been away. As for his education, there is nothing for you to worry about: his ability you know, and his application I can see.Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.14

  • Magna nōbīs puerīs, Quīnte frāter, sī memoriā tenēs, opīniō fuit L. Crassum nōn plūs attigisse doctrīnae quam quantum prīma illa puerīlī īnstitūtiōne potuisset; M. autem Antōnium omnīnō omnis ērudītiōnis expertem atque ignārum fuisse

    When we were boys, brother Quintus, if you remember, it was widely believed that Lucius Crassus had acquired no more learning than his first schooling could give him, and that Marcus Antonius had had no education at allCic. de Or. 2.1

  • ut ager quamvīs fertilis sine cultūrā frūctuōsus esse nōn potest, sīc sine doctrīnā animus

    as a field, however fertile, cannot bear fruit without cultivation, so a mind cannot without educationCic. Tusc. 2.13

See also school, teacher, student, learn, university, subject.
